report:
Finding
- The finetuning appears to have produced no measurable behavioral change. In other words, there is no clear finetuning objective that was successfully instilled — Model B is effectively the same as Model A.

Reasoning from the evidence
1. Difference norms: every (layer, position) cell shows an L2 norm of 0.000. That indicates the residual-stream activation difference B − A is essentially zero (within measurement/rounding noise) at all inspected layers and positions. If the finetuning had meaningfully changed the model, we would expect non‑zero concentrated signals in some layers/positions.

2. Logit‑lens outputs: the top tokens pointed to by the difference vectors are generic, very-high-frequency tokens/characters such as " o", "is", "it", " p", " t", "\n", "in", " a", "or", " s". When the activation difference is vanishingly small, projections into vocabulary space tend to be dominated by common-token directions or numerical noise; they do not show any task‑specific or domain‑specific token preference. The repetition of the same small set of common tokens across many layers/positions is consistent with either a near-zero difference or noise, not a coherent new objective.

3. Patchscope readouts: no distinctive continuations are reported. Injecting the difference into an identity prompt produced no recognizable behavioral signature, again consistent with negligible change.

Conclusion and caveats
- The most parsimonious conclusion is that the finetuning either (a) failed (e.g., zero/very small learning rate, no update), (b) was trivially small (too few steps or tiny dataset) so its effect is below measurement noise, or (c) explicitly optimized for identity/no-change. Any real, nontrivial finetuning objective would almost certainly leave detectable activation differences and more distinctive logit/continuation signatures.

Confidence: high, given the near‑zero norms and lack of any task‑specific signals.
